title: Leaders Who Ask for Your Opinion But Really Don't Want It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership identifies a pervasive leadership failure pattern they call 'inquiry theatre': leaders who habitually seek input from their teams without any genuine openness to being influenced. This pattern rarely starts as manipulation -- it usually begins with strong convictions or a belief that consensus equals compromise -- but over time it trains teams to stop bringing their best thinking, to agree passively with whatever the leader already thinks, and to grow suspicious of any question the leader asks. The real cost is not bad decisions but the destruction of candor: team members learn to keep their true opinions to themselves, trust breaks down, and the leader loses access to the honest feedback needed to reality-test conclusions. The article distinguishes false openness from the legitimate practice of stress-testing a conclusion: good leaders can share a preliminary position and honestly invite objections or risks they have not imagined -- the problem is pretending to be open when the matter is already settled. Almost every leader falls into false inquiry occasionally; the differentiator is whether the leader recognizes the pattern and breaks it immediately, or allows it to calcify into a team norm that permanently suppresses candor.
points: Inquiry theatre destroys candor incrementally: once team members learn that input does not matter, they stop offering genuine views and begin performing agreement instead, permanently degrading the leader's access to honest feedback.

The critical distinction is between false openness (asking while having no intention of being influenced) and honest stress-testing (sharing a preliminary conclusion and genuinely inviting objections or risks not yet imagined) -- the latter is legitimate, the former is manipulative.

Trust, once lost through inquiry theatre, changes everything about how the team functions: members become suspicious of the real intent behind any question the leader asks, including genuine ones, and the damage is hard to reverse.

Good leaders do not ask questions they already know the answer to -- they seek input only on issues and decisions they remain genuinely open to, and they make explicit what has already been decided versus what is still open for influence.

Almost every leader falls into false inquiry occasionally; the differentiator is immediate recognition and breaking the pattern before it becomes a team norm -- habitual inquiry theatre is a leadership identity problem, not just a communication style.
quotes: Some leaders feign that they are interested in what others think about an issue when, in fact, they have little interest or have already made the decision.
Over time, the leader settles into a pattern: consulting the team without any genuine openness to influence.
The real cost isn't typically bad decisions or missteps. It's the negative impact this inquiry theatre has on how the team engages.

Once team members learn that their input isn't taken seriously, they stop bringing their best thinking and offering their candid views. Trust breaks down, and they become suspicious about the real intent behind any question the leader asks.

Entering any conversation with a conclusion that can't be influenced is bad form. Once the matter has been settled in the leader's mind, any conversation seeking input is a facade that undermines the leader's credibility.
In some cases, good leaders admit they've reached a conclusion and just want to stress-test it for any unimagined risks or objections. That seems reasonable to the team.
Leaders who ask for input without any intention of being influenced teach people to keep their true opinions to themselves. Candor across the team suffers tremendously.
